doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Family attitudes and sitting in with Stanford East and Don Ewell
summary: His eccentric family, sitting in with Stanford East's small group and following Don Ewell's Dixieland band.

bands.name: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Okay. Well you found yourself pursuing music, I wonder if your parents were in favor of that?

Oh well my father was a very creative duck. He was very eccentric and I was well prepared for all the crazy people I was going to be involved with. My whole family is a little bit crazy, except my sister, she was a straight arrow. And my brother went to a place — you probably never heard of — Black Mountain College, but that was a place in North Carolina, it was almost like a commune. And they had really prestigious people teaching there but it was very small. Anyhow no, they weren’t. My mother was sure I would starve to death and my father was an advertising person. He was successful and very creative, but a real individual. And he alternately encouraged me and discouraged me. So that’s a psychological thing. But what happened was I got more and more passionately involved with the music. And I used to spend a lot of time in the black section of Baltimore sitting in with some fantastic local players, who incidentally, every city had or probably has these people. You’d hear Miles or Dizzy or this one talk about this great guy in this town that never left. In other words somebody like Wes Montgomery would have never left Indianapolis if Cannonball hadn’t found him and pushed him out there, that kind of thing. So I used to sit in with a trumpet player named Stanford East, and he had this little quintet that was a cross between the Louis Jordan Tympani Five and the Basie small group.

No, like the records that made “Shoeshine Boy” and all that. They had that kind of feel. And that grabbed me. Because on the other side of town they were playing Dixieland or whatever they called it. But there was a great pianist I used to follow around who made a big reputation, his name was Don Ewell. E-W-E-L-L. And his brother was a trombone player. They had a band that sounded like Bob Crosby’s Bobcats. A terrific band.
